hypothesis: An adversary who compromised Windows hosts in this network stole credentials from them (MITRE ATT&CK tactic: Credential Access).

frame.restated: An adversary with existing access to Windows hosts on this network is stealing credentials from those hosts.
frame.what_would_confirm: Observable evidence such as LSASS process memory access (e.g., via Mimikatz or procdump), suspicious access to SAM/SECURITY registry hives, use of Windows Credential Manager APIs, or anomalous authentication events indicating credential theft.
frame.what_would_refute: Absence of any credential dumping tool execution, no unauthorized access to LSASS or registry hives, and no anomalous credential-related events on the compromised Windows hosts.

verdict.rationale: 7 in-scope incident(s) of verified malicious findings (confidence >= medium): I01 T1003.001 (F01, F10, F22, F25, F35, F37, F39, F45), I02 T1003.001 (F57), I03 T1003.002 (F31, F56), I04 T1187 (F23), I06 T1552.001 (F58), I07 T1555.003 (F59), I09 T1649 (F54)
verdict.rule: Confirmed if >=1 in-scope incident of verified malicious findings (confidence >= medium); Inconclusive if only suspicious incidents or coverage gaps; Refuted if full coverage and no malicious/suspicious finding

T1003.name: OS Credential Dumping
T1003.reason: LSASS memory was opened with full-access masks (0x1F3FFF/0x1FFFFF) by attacker-controlled PowerShell on scranton and wsmprovhost on nashua, consistent with OS credential dumping.

T1003.001.name: LSASS Memory
T1003.001.reason: lsass.exe created C:\Windows\debug\PASSWD.LOG on scranton at 03:19:09, consistent with credential material written by LSASS.

T1003.002.name: Security Account Manager
T1003.002.reason: pspasswd64/pspasswd.exe written to Downloads by PowerShell and accesschk.exe created 'passwordsDB' on scranton — local credential collection tooling.

T1003.003.name: NTDS
T1003.003.reason: No ntds/NTDS.dit file creation, no ntdsutil/vssadmin/diskshadow command lines, no shadow-copy artifacts.

T1003.004.name: LSA Secrets
T1003.004.reason: No lsadump/secrets command lines, no SECURITY Policy Secrets handle requests, no LSA-secret PowerShell blocks.

T1003.005.name: Cached Domain Credentials
T1003.005.reason: No non-lsass access to Cache/SECURITY objects and no mscache/DCC2/cached-credential references.

T1003.006.name: DCSync
T1003.006.reason: No drsuapi/dcsync/lsadump command lines or PowerShell script blocks indicating directory replication abuse.

T1040.name: Network Sniffing
T1040.reason: The only packet-capture activity is the legitimate Azure NetworkWatcherAgent.exe invoking 'netsh trace start capture=yes' on scranton.dmevals.local (SYSTEM, parent services.exe), immediately followed by 'netsh trace stop'. No sniffing tools (tcpdump/windump/wireshark/rawcap/dumpcap), no pcap/npcap/winpcap driver loads, and no promiscuous-mode/raw-socket indicators were found in windows.sysmon, windows.security, windows.powershell or windows.other. The malicious activity present in the window (PsExec lateral movement with plaintext creds, python.exe C2 to 192.168.0.4:8443, screen capture, steganography, sdelete) is not network sniffing.

T1056.name: Input Capture
T1056.reason: Active intrusion chain on scranton.dmevals.local: malicious .scr -> cmd -> hidden bypassed PowerShell decoding monkey.png payload, Invoke-Discovery/Invoke-Exfil, sdelete64 cleanup, culminating in full-access LSASS handle.

T1056.001.name: Keylogging
T1056.001.reason: No keylogger command lines, script blocks, or hooking APIs found; LSASS/winlogon accesses are benign 0x1000 query-limited-info from system processes.

T1056.002.name: GUI Input Capture
T1056.002.reason: No GUI input-capture tooling or credential-prompt process creations observed.

T1056.003.name: Web Portal Capture
T1056.003.reason: No web portal/login/wwwroot/inetpub artifacts, no IIS processes, no HTTP POST or login URLs in zeek.

T1056.004.name: Credential API Hooking
T1056.004.reason: PowerShell.exe opened lsass.exe with GrantedAccess 0x1FFFFF (PROCESS_ALL_ACCESS) and read it with AccessMask 0x10 on scranton, consistent with credential API hooking/memory read for credential theft.

T1110.name: Brute Force
T1110.reason: No 4625/4740/4771 events; only a successful 4776 (Status 0x0) and benign logon notifications. No brute-force pattern.

T1110.001.name: Password Guessing
T1110.001.reason: Zero failed logons; PowerShell 'password' hits are credential theft/exfil scripts (Get-PrivateKeys, Invoke-Exfil), not guessing.

T1110.002.name: Password Cracking
T1110.002.reason: SAM hive accessed only by lsass.exe itself (AccessMask 0xf003f); lsass handle opens are normal svchost/AV agents; no cracking tools or wordlist/potfile artifacts.

T1110.003.name: Password Spraying
T1110.003.reason: No failed logons or lockouts; 4648 explicit-credential logons are PsExec lateral movement by pbeesly, not spraying.

T1110.004.name: Credential Stuffing
T1110.004.reason: No repeated authentication attempts against multiple accounts; only one successful 4776 credential validation.

T1111.name: Multi-Factor Authentication Interception
T1111.reason: No MFA interception activity found. All 'Credential' matches are benign Windows internals (Credential Guard config, CredentialEnrollmentManager service registration, MuiCache). No smart-card/OTP/token-provider or credential-provider interception artifacts. The credential-related activity present (LSASS high-access reads by PowerShell/wsmprovhost, and a PowerShell exfil script using a hardcoded credential) belongs to other techniques (T1003/T1041), not T1111.

T1187.name: Forced Authentication
T1187.reason: Host 10.0.1.4 (scranton) was coerced into authenticating to attacker-controlled 192.168.0.4: SMB/445 attempts were rejected (REJ), then the Windows WebDAV redirector (Microsoft-WebDAV-MiniRedir/10.0.18362) issued OPTIONS/PROPFIND/PUT/LOCK/PROPPATCH/HEAD/UNLOCK to http://192.168.0.4/webdav/, creating /webdav/OfficeSupplies.7z (PUT 201) with an AUTHORIZATION header present - credential leakage via forced authentication.

T1212.name: Exploitation for Credential Access
T1212.reason: On nashua.dmevals.local at 2020-05-02T03:09:29, PowerShell Remoting host wsmprovhost.exe (SYSTEM) opened a full-access (0x1F3FFF) handle to lsass.exe and to many other processes (winlogon, vssvc, Sysmon, svchost), immediately following the operator command 'Invoke-SeaDukeStage -ComputerName NASHUA' from scranton.dmevals.local (user pbeesly). This is consistent with exploitation-driven credential access / process dumping within an active intrusion.

T1539.name: Steal Web Session Cookie
T1539.reason: All cookie-related hits are benign: WebDAV DavSetCookie (davclnt.dll) process creations on scranton.dmevals.local and a Windows WARP JIT service INetCookies file creation. No access to browser cookie databases (Chrome/Edge/Firefox Cookies, Login Data, Web Data) was found in Sysmon file-creation, Sysmon process-access, Security 4663 object-access, or PowerShell script-block data. The credential activity in the window is password-based lateral movement via PsExec, not web session cookie theft.

T1552.name: Unsecured Credentials
T1552.reason: pbeesly on scranton ran Sysinternals accesschk.exe which created a file named 'passwordsDB', alongside sdelete64 artifact wiping, indicating credential-access tooling.

T1552.001.name: Credentials In Files
T1552.001.reason: Invoke-Exfil script embeds plaintext credential cozy/MyCozyPassw0rd! used to mount attacker WebDAV share for exfil.

T1552.002.name: Credentials in Registry
T1552.002.reason: All Password/Credential registry writes were by svchost/lsass/services/winlogon OS components, not adversary activity.

T1552.003.name: Shell History
T1552.003.reason: No consolehost_history or shell history file access in sysmon or security datasets.

T1552.004.name: Private Keys
T1552.004.reason: Get-PrivateKeys exported LocalMachine certificates to .pfx (coyn5igj.3io.pfx) on scranton — private key material theft (already anchored as T1649).

T1552.006.name: Group Policy Preferences
T1552.006.reason: GptTmpl.inf/sysvol GPP file access was performed by svchost.exe Group Policy processing and routine SMB GPO retrieval; no Groups.xml cpassword abuse.

T1555.name: Credentials from Password Stores
T1555.reason: PowerShell.exe (pbeesly) on scranton opened lsass.exe with 0x1FFFFF/0x1F3FFF and wsmprovhost.exe (pbeesly) on nashua opened lsass.exe with 0x1F3FFF, both including 'Read from process memory' (Sysmon 10 + Security 4656), the classic LSASS credential-dumping access pattern.

T1555.003.name: Credentials from Web Browsers
T1555.003.reason: Password-protected Rar archive of collected data staged on nashua then wiped with sdelete; consistent with browser/credential store harvesting but the source files were not directly observed.

T1555.004.name: Windows Credential Manager
T1555.004.reason: Full-access LSASS handles by pbeesly's PowerShell/wsmprovhost are the mechanism for harvesting Credential Manager/DPAPI secrets from LSASS memory; no explicit vaultcmd/cmdkey usage seen.

T1555.005.name: Password Managers
T1555.005.reason: No password-manager executables, files or script references (keepass/1password/bitwarden/lastpass/kdbx) in any dataset.

T1556.name: Modify Authentication Process
T1556.reason: PowerShell.exe on scranton.dmevals.local opened lsass.exe with 0x1fffff/0x1f3fff (PROCESS_ALL_ACCESS) at 03:05:16, and user pbeesly ran a malicious PowerShell chain (registry-stored payload via HKLM:\SOFTWARE\Javasoft -> Invoke-Expression, obfuscated GetProcAddress P/Invoke, Gzip+Base64 hidden launcher) at 03:21:27-03:21:29. This is credential theft from the authentication process rather than modification of it, so the family-level activity is suspicious/malicious but no authentication-process tampering was seen.

T1556.001.name: Domain Controller Authentication
T1556.001.reason: LogonType 3 4624 events are routine machine-account Kerberos logons (NEWYORK$, SCRANTON$, NASHUA$, UTICA$, WEC$); no DC authentication backdoor or Skeleton-Key-style anomaly was found.

T1556.002.name: Password Filter DLL
T1556.002.reason: No 4657 registry change to Notification Packages/lsass keys, no 4688/4104 referencing password filter DLLs.

T1556.005.name: Reversible Encryption
T1556.005.reason: No 4739, no Reversible/Set-ADUser/dsmod command lines, no AllowReversiblePasswordEncryption references.

T1556.006.name: Multi-Factor Authentication
T1556.006.reason: No 4739/5136/4738 and no Set-ADUser/Set-ADAccountControl activity indicating MFA modification.

T1556.007.name: Hybrid Identity
T1556.007.reason: No 5136/4739/4738 and no Connect-MsolService or cloud-identity cmdlet usage.

T1556.008.name: Network Provider DLL
T1556.008.reason: No 4657 NetworkProvider/Credential registry changes and no PowerShell referencing NetworkProvider DLLs.

T1557.name: Adversary-in-the-Middle
T1557.reason: No AiTM positioning observed; the only network anomaly (placeholder responder MAC 12:34:56:78:9a:bc answering for many IPs) is a zeek capture artifact, and SMB/RPC traffic is normal domain activity.

T1557.001.name: Name Resolution Poisoning and SMB Relay
T1557.001.reason: No LLMNR/NBT-NS poisoning or SMB relay; DNS queries are normal, no Responder/MITM tooling in PowerShell, and 4697 service installs are built-in services plus PSEXESVC/javamtsup (lateral movement, not relay).

T1557.002.name: ARP Cache Poisoning
T1557.002.reason: No ARP cache poisoning; duplicate MAC-to-IP mappings in zeek are capture artifacts (synthetic placeholder MAC), and no ARP/netsh manipulation appears in PowerShell.

T1557.003.name: DHCP Spoofing
T1557.003.reason: No DHCP telemetry exists in any dataset: no dhcp log type in zeek, no DHCP event codes in windows.other, no ports 67/68 in Sysmon, no DHCP strings in PowerShell.

T1558.name: Steal or Forge Kerberos Tickets
T1558.reason: PowerShell.exe on scranton opened lsass.exe with GrantedAccess 0x1FFFFF and wsmprovhost.exe on nashua opened lsass.exe with 0x1F3FFF, following a fileless registry->Invoke-Expression loader and reflective shellcode loader run by pbeesly — credential access targeting Kerberos ticket material in LSASS.

T1558.001.name: Golden Ticket
T1558.001.reason: SCRANTON$@DMEVALS.LOCAL requested krbtgt service tickets (Service ID ...-502, TicketOptions 0x60810010) on newyork.dmevals.local, an unusual TGS request pattern consistent with forged/abused ticket activity; no RC4 downgrade seen.

T1558.002.name: Silver Ticket
T1558.002.reason: All 4769 service tickets were KDC-issued with AES256 (0x12) and normal options; no forged service-ticket usage artifacts found.

T1558.003.name: Kerberoasting
T1558.003.reason: Zeek Kerberos shows only normal AS/TGS traffic with preauth required; no mass SPN requests, RC4 downgrade, or Kerberoast tooling strings.

T1558.004.name: AS-REP Roasting
T1558.004.reason: All AS requests returned KDC_ERR_PREAUTH_REQUIRED; no AS-REP roasting tooling or preauth-disabled accounts observed.

T1606.name: Forge Web Credentials
T1606.reason: No forged web credential material. Keyword hits in PowerShell 4104 are benign Sysinternals readme.ps1 and PowerShellGet resource strings; LSASS access with high masks comes from legitimate SYSTEM processes (wininit/csrss/svchost) and a SYSTEM PowerShell with a normal ntdll/KERNELBASE call trace.

T1606.001.name: Web Cookies
T1606.001.reason: Only cookie-path file event is a benign Windows service-profile INetCookies file created by svchost.exe; no browser cookie theft or Set-Cookie/session manipulation found.

T1606.002.name: SAML Tokens
T1606.002.reason: Zero hits for SAML/Assertion/NotOnOrAfter in PowerShell, no saml/token/cert command lines in Sysmon, no saml/adfs/token URLs in Zeek HTTP.

T1621.name: Multi-Factor Authentication Request Generation
T1621.reason: No MFA request generation activity found. The only hit (C355, windows.other 5857/5858) is routine WMI provider startup and RSOP DeleteInstance cleanup by SYSTEM on newyork.dmevals.local. No 4625 failed logons in windows.security, no MFA/2FA/authenticator strings in PowerShell script blocks or Sysmon command lines, and no MFA-related HTTP URLs in zeek.

T1649.name: Steal or Forge Authentication Certificates
T1649.reason: PowerShell Get-PrivateKeys on scranton.dmevals.local (user pbeesly) enumerated cert:\LocalMachine and exported certificates to a password-protected .pfx in Downloads (confirmed by Sysmon file-create of coyn5igj.3io.pfx by powershell.exe PID 3876 and concurrent reads of the MY\Certificates Blob registry keys), followed by an Invoke-BeachCleanup function deleting the .pfx files. This is theft of authentication certificates/private keys.

checks.purpose: Stack all process creations to spot credential-dumping tools (mimikatz, procdump, comsvcs.dll rundll32) among rare executables.
Stack process-access targets to find LSASS or other credential-store processes being opened.
Stack object types accessed under handle/object-access auditing to find SAM/SECURITY/LSASS objects.
Stack newly created processes to spot dumping utilities launched on hosts.

args.query: event.code:4104 AND (powershell.script_block_text:*lsass* OR powershell.script_block_text:*mimikatz* OR powershell.script_block_text:*sekurlsa* OR powershell.script_block_text:*DumpCreds*)

checks.purpose: Find PowerShell script blocks referencing LSASS/credential-dumping APIs.
Look for credential-dumping references in other Windows event channels (service installs, VSS, etc.).
Stack granted-access masks on LSASS process opens to reveal memory-read access typical of dumping.
Read individual LSASS access events with source image and granted access.

args.query: FROM logs-windows.sysmon-default METADATA _id, _index | WHERE event.code == "10" AND (TO_LOWER(win.TargetImage) LIKE "*chrome.exe" OR TO_LOWER(win.TargetImage) LIKE "*firefox.exe" OR TO_LOWER(win.TargetImage) LIKE "*msedge.exe" OR TO_LOWER(win.TargetImage) LIKE "*iexplore.exe") | KEEP @timestamp, host.name, user.name, win.SourceImage, win.TargetImage, win.GrantedAccess, _id, _index

checks.purpose: Process-access events (Sysmon 10) against browser processes indicate memory-based browser credential theft.

args.query: FROM logs-windows.security-default METADATA _id, _index | WHERE event.code IN ("4663","4656","4658") AND (TO_LOWER(win.ObjectName) LIKE "*login data*" OR TO_LOWER(win.ObjectName) LIKE "*logins.json*" OR TO_LOWER(win.ObjectName) LIKE "*key3.db*" OR TO_LOWER(win.ObjectName) LIKE "*key4.db*" OR TO_LOWER(win.ObjectName) LIKE "*google*chrome*user data*" OR TO_LOWER(win.ObjectName) LIKE "*mozilla*firefox*profiles*") | KEEP @timestamp, host.name, user.name, win.ObjectName, win.ProcessName, _id, _index

checks.purpose: Object-access auditing on browser credential-store files shows a process reading them.

args.query: FROM logs-windows.powershell-default METADATA _id, _index | WHERE event.code IN ("4103","4104") AND (TO_LOWER(COALESCE(powershell.script_block_text, win.ScriptBlockText, "")) LIKE "*login data*" OR TO_LOWER(COALESCE(powershell.script_block_text, win.ScriptBlockText, "")) LIKE "*logins.json*" OR TO_LOWER(COALESCE(powershell.script_block_text, win.ScriptBlockText, "")) LIKE "*key3.db*" OR TO_LOWER(COALESCE(powershell.script_block_text, win.ScriptBlockText, "")) LIKE "*key4.db*" OR TO_LOWER(COALESCE(powershell.script_block_text, win.ScriptBlockText, "")) LIKE "*sharpchrome*" OR TO_LOWER(COALESCE(powershell.script_block_text, win.ScriptBlockText, "")) LIKE "*lazagne*") | KEEP @timestamp, host.name, user.name, powershell.script_block_text, _id, _index

checks.purpose: PowerShell scripts targeting browser credential stores or running browser-credential extraction modules.

args.query: FROM logs-windows.other-default METADATA _id, _index | WHERE TO_LOWER(COALESCE(message, win.Message, "")) LIKE "*login data*" OR TO_LOWER(COALESCE(message, win.Message, "")) LIKE "*logins.json*" OR TO_LOWER(COALESCE(message, win.Message, "")) LIKE "*chrome*" OR TO_LOWER(COALESCE(message, win.Message, "")) LIKE "*firefox*" | KEEP @timestamp, host.name, event.code, message, _id, _index

checks.purpose: Other Windows channels may log browser credential-store file access or browser-related activity.
Detect processes opening handles to lsass.exe, which is how Credential Manager secrets (DPAPI vaults) are commonly harvested.

findings.title: LSASS memory accessed with full-access mask (0x1F3FFF) by attacker PowerShell on scranton and via WinRM on nashua
findings.summary: On scranton.dmevals.local, PowerShell.exe (PID 2976, user pbeesly) opened lsass.exe (PID 736) with GrantedAccess 0x1F3FFF at 2020-05-02T03:05:16.623Z, and again with 0x1FFFFF at 03:05:16.654Z. The matching Security 4656 event (record 73759) shows the same process requesting AccessMask 0x1F3FFF on \Device\HarddiskVolume2\Windows\System32\lsass.exe, explicitly including 'Read from process memory' and 'Write to process memory' — the access pattern of an LSASS memory dump. This occurred inside a pbeesly PowerShell session that also ran attacker tooling (Invoke-Discovery, Invoke-Persistence, Get-PrivateKeys, Invoke-ScreenCapture, accesschk.exe). On nashua.dmevals.local, wsmprovhost.exe (PID 7720, WinRM remote PowerShell, user pbeesly) opened lsass.exe (PID 728) with GrantedAccess 0x1F3FFF at 03:09:29.430Z, the same full-access LSASS read via remote PowerShell. The remaining LSASS opens (svchost.exe 0x1000, WindowsAzureTelemetryService.exe 0x1400, wininit/csrss at process start) are normal system behaviour.

findings.title: lsass.exe wrote C:\Windows\debug\PASSWD.LOG on scranton
findings.summary: On scranton.dmevals.local at 03:19:09, lsass.exe (pid 748, SYSTEM) created C:\Windows\debug\PASSWD.LOG. A password log written by lsass in the debug directory is consistent with credential material being written out during the intrusion window, distinct from the previously anchored LSASS handle-access findings.

findings.title: Sysinternals pspasswd downloaded and accesschk used to create 'passwordsDB' on scranton
findings.summary: On scranton.dmevals.local, PowerShell (pid 3876, user pbeesly) wrote Sysinternals pspasswd64.exe/pspasswd.exe into C:\Users\pbeesly\Downloads\SysinternalsSuite at 03:00:28-03:00:32, then accesschk.exe (pid 9204) created a file named 'passwordsDB' in C:\Program Files\SysinternalsSuite at 03:04:35. pspasswd is a password-reset/credential tool and the 'passwordsDB' artifact indicates local account credential material was being collected on the host.

On scranton.dmevals.local a malicious screen-saver C:\ProgramData\victim\...cod.3aka3.scr was launched from explorer.exe, spawning cmd.exe then powershell.exe. The PowerShell session (user pbeesly) executed a hidden, execution-policy-bypassed command that decoded a payload from C:\Users\pbeesly\Downloads\monkey.png, compiled code with csc.exe, ran Invoke-Discovery and Invoke-Exfil (which embeds a hardcoded credential and exfiltrates to \\192.168.0.4\webdav), and deleted the .scr with sdelete64.exe. This is the surrounding credential-access campaign context.

findings.summary: On scranton.dmevals.local, PowerShell.exe (PID 2976) opened C:\windows\system32\lsass.exe with GrantedAccess 0x1FFFFF (PROCESS_ALL_ACCESS) at 2020-05-02T03:05:16.654Z, and a 4663 event at 03:05:16 records the same powershell.exe reading lsass with AccessMask 0x10 (PROCESS_VM_READ). This is the credential-access step of an active intrusion: the same host/user (pbeesly) ran a hidden, execution-policy-bypassed PowerShell payload decoded from monkey.png, compiled code via csc.exe, ran Invoke-Discovery and Invoke-Exfil, and cleaned up with sdelete64.exe. Full-access handle to LSASS is the hallmark of credential API hooking / memory read for credential theft.
findings.title: PowerShell opens LSASS with PROCESS_ALL_ACCESS (0x1FFFFF) on scranton during intrusion chain

findings.summary: On 2020-04-30 between 00:32:14 and 00:32:22, host 10.0.1.4 (scranton.dmevals.local) attempted SMB to 192.168.0.4 on port 445 and was rejected (conn_state REJ, history 'Sr', 5 attempts 00:32:14.891-00:32:17.069). It then fell back to WebDAV over HTTP port 80 using the Windows WebDAV redirector (user_agent 'Microsoft-WebDAV-MiniRedir/10.0.18362'), issuing OPTIONS/PROPFIND/PUT/LOCK/PROPPATCH/HEAD/UNLOCK against http://192.168.0.4/webdav/ and successfully creating /webdav/OfficeSupplies.7z (PUT -> 201 Created). The PUT request carried an AUTHORIZATION header, i.e. the victim host transmitted credentials to the attacker-controlled server. This is the classic T1187 forced-authentication pattern: a UNC/WebDAV path (\\192.168.0.4\webdav\OfficeSupplies.7z) coerces the victim into authenticating to an attacker listener, leaking NTLM material. The activity is preceded by PowerShell Gallery / oneget CDN access (www.powershellgallery.com, onegetcdn.azureedge.net, go.microsoft.com at 00:31-00:32), consistent with a package-install or scripted workflow used to trigger the coercion. findings.summary: The overwhelming majority of Sysmon event.code 10 process-access events (39283 total) are C:\windows\system32\svchost.exe opening handles with GrantedAccess 0x1000 (PROCESS_QUERY_LIMITED_INFORMATION) to other svchost.exe instances and to lsass.exe. This is normal Windows service-host behaviour (e.g. service status queries) and is not indicative of credential-access exploitation. The anomalous outlier is the wsmprovhost.exe 0x1f3fff burst reported separately.
findings.title: svchost.exe 0x1000 process-access events are routine Windows behaviour
WebDAV DavSetCookie activity is not browser session-cookie theft
findings.summary: On scranton.dmevals.local, user pbeesly spawned rundll32.exe running davclnt.dll,DavSetCookie against 192.168.0.4 http://192.168.0.4/webdav (5 process-creation events, 2020-05-01T23:08:50 to 23:10:23 local). This is the Windows WebDAV client setting a WebDAV authentication cookie for a mounted WebDAV share, not theft of a browser web session cookie. The parent process is svchost.exe and the command line contains no browser profile or cookie-database path.

findings.title: INetCookies file creation is a Windows WARP JIT service artifact
findings.summary: The only Sysmon file-creation event matching *cookie* is svchost.exe (PID 7200, SYSTEM) creating C:\Windows\ServiceProfiles\LocalService\AppData\Local\Packages\warp_jit_db4a1097-b484-4973-bbf2-a04208ecd4d4\AC\INetCookies on scranton.dmevals.local at 2020-05-02T03:21:05.681Z. This is the Windows WARP JIT service package's own INetCookies store under the LocalService service profile, not a browser cookie database (no Chrome/Edge/Firefox profile path).

findings.title: No access to browser cookie stores or credential-stealer tooling
findings.summary: Targeted hunts found no theft of web session cookies. Sysmon file-creation (event 11) matching *cookies*/*login data*/*web data*/*cookies.sqlite* returned only the single WARP JIT INetCookies artifact; Sysmon process-access (event 10) to Edge/Chrome/Firefox/IEXPLORE targets returned only routine Explorer.EXE and svchost.exe read accesses (GrantedAccess 0x2000/0x3000) consistent with normal browser launch; Security 4663 object-access to cookie/login-data/browser paths returned zero rows; PowerShell script blocks matching *cookie*/*login data* returned zero rows. The credential-related activity present in the window is password-based lateral movement (PsExec64.exe with a cleartext password to \\NASHUA), which is not T1539.

Sysmon event 13 registry value sets matching Password/Credential were all written by legitimate system processes: svchost.exe writing HKU\.DEFAULT\Software\Microsoft\IdentityCRL\ProviderPasswordLength/CharacterGroups, lsass.exe writing the DeviceGuard CredentialGuard Enabled value, services.exe creating the CredentialEnrollmentManagerUserSvc service keys, and winlogon.exe writing Winlogon\PasswordExpiryNotification. None represent an adversary storing or reading credentials in the registry.
findings.title: Registry Password/Credential value sets are OS-internal, not credential harvesting

findings.summary: Sysmon file-creation events for GptTmpl.inf and the sysvol GroupPolicy DataStore path on scranton.dmevals.local and nashua.dmevals.local were all generated by C:\windows\system32\svchost.exe (the Group Policy client), which is normal Windows Group Policy refresh behavior. Zeek smb_files records show SMB FILE_OPEN of \\NEWYORK.dmevals.local\sysvol ...\GptTmpl.inf from 10.0.1.4 and 10.0.1.6, also consistent with routine GPO retrieval. No Groups.xml with cpassword was observed and no non-standard process read these files.
findings.title: Group Policy Preferences / SecEdit files accessed only by normal svchost Group Policy processing
Benign LSASS access by system processes and Azure guest tooling
findings.summary: Most LSASS handle events are routine: wininit.exe/csrss.exe opening lsass.exe with 0x1FFFFF at scranton 03:19:09 (process startup), svchost.exe with 0x101001, CollectGuestLogs.exe (C:\WindowsAzure\Packages) with 0x1410/0x10 on scranton/utica/newyork/nashua, and Windows Defender MsMpEng.exe with 0x1FFFFF on scranton. The sdelete64.exe LSASS event on nashua is LSASS (SourceImage lsass.exe) accessing sdelete64.exe via lsasrv.dll/SspiSrv.dll/RPCRT4.dll — normal SSPI/RPC, not sdelete reading LSASS. These are expected system behaviours, not credential theft.

findings.title: No browser credential-store access observed
findings.summary: Checks for browser credential artifacts (Login Data, logins.json, cookies) in Sysmon process/file events, Security object access, PowerShell script blocks and other channels returned no hits. The only file event matching a cookie path was a benign system file (INetCookies under the LocalService WARP JIT package profile) on scranton, not a browser credential store. No evidence of web-browser credential theft in the available windows.sysmon/security/powershell/other data.

The 218 LogonType 3 (network) 4624 events are dominated by machine-account Kerberos logons: NEWYORK$ (from ::1, fe80::e40c:95b6:b0a7:6429, 10.0.0.4), SCRANTON$ (10.0.1.4), NASHUA$ (10.0.1.6), UTICA$ (10.0.1.5) and WEC$ (10.0.1.10), all with LogonProcessName 'Kerberos'. These are routine computer-account authentications between domain members and the DC, not evidence of a DC authentication backdoor. The only non-machine account is pbeesly (13 logons from 10.0.1.4, 5 with no source, 1 from 10.0.1.6, 1 NtLmSsp from 172.18.39.2), consistent with the compromised user's lateral movement rather than a modified DC authentication process. No 4648 explicit-credential logon to a domain controller or Skeleton Key-style anomaly was observed.
findings.title: Machine-account Kerberos network logons (normal DC authentication, no backdoor)
No adversary-in-the-middle activity observed; Zeek MAC anomalies are capture artifacts
findings.summary: Across windows.security, windows.sysmon, windows.other, windows.powershell and zeek there is no evidence of an adversary positioned in the middle. The only network-level oddity is in the zeek capture (2020-04-30 window): responder MAC 12:34:56:78:9a:bc answers for many unrelated destination IPs (192.168.0.4, 10.0.0.4, 10.0.1.6, 192.168.0.5) and source 10.0.1.4 appears with two MACs (00:0d:3a:4d:42:f2 and fc:bd:67:e1:a9:c1). 12:34:56:78:9a:bc is a synthetic/placeholder MAC, so this is a capture artifact rather than a real host impersonating others. SMB/RPC traffic is normal domain activity (SAMR/LSAR to the DC, IPC$ mapping).

findings.title: No name-resolution poisoning or SMB relay; service installs are built-in/PSEXESVC
findings.summary: Sysmon DNS queries (event 22) show only normal lookups (host FQDNs, LDAP SRV records, Microsoft telemetry, wpad) with no LLMNR/NBT-NS-style poisoning, and no Responder/MITM/LLMNR/NBT-NS strings appear in PowerShell script blocks. The 23 event.code 4697 service installations are Windows built-in per-user services (svchost UnistackSvcGroup etc.) plus PSEXESVC (%SystemRoot%\PSEXESVC.exe, installed by user pbeesly on nashua) and javamtsup (C:\Windows\System32\javamtsup.exe on scranton) — these are lateral-movement/execution artifacts, not SMB relay. Zeek SMB/RPC is normal domain traffic.

findings.title: No ARP cache poisoning; duplicate MAC-to-IP mappings are capture artifacts
findings.summary: Stacking source and responder MACs in the zeek conn log shows no host claiming multiple IPs in a way consistent with ARP spoofing. Source 10.0.1.4 appears with two MACs (00:0d:3a:4d:42:f2 and fc:bd:67:e1:a9:c1) and the responder 12:34:56:78:9a:bc (a synthetic placeholder MAC) answers for several distinct IPs — both are artifacts of the capture rather than gratuitous ARP. No ARP/netsh interface manipulation appears in PowerShell script blocks, and no ARP-related object access stands out in windows.security.

findings.title: No silver-ticket evidence observed
findings.summary: The 4769 service-ticket requests on newyork.dmevals.local were all issued by the KDC with encryption type 0x12 (AES256) and normal TicketOptions; no service tickets were observed being used without a corresponding KDC-issued request, and no forged service-ticket artifacts (e.g. anomalous SPN usage) were found. No silver-ticket activity is evident in the retrieved events.

findings.title: No Kerberoasting pattern observed
findings.summary: Zeek Kerberos records (2020-04-30 window, non-overlapping with the Windows data) show only normal pbeesly AS/TGS traffic to krbtgt, cifs/NASHUA, host/nashua.dmevals.local, HTTP/NASHUA and ldap/NEWYORK, with KDC_ERR_PREAUTH_REQUIRED on AS requests. No mass SPN service-ticket requests or RC4 (etype 23) downgrade typical of Kerberoasting were seen, and no Kerberoast/Rubeus/Invoke-Kerberoast strings appeared in PowerShell script blocks.

findings.title: No AS-REP Roasting evidence observed
findings.summary: Zeek Kerberos AS requests all returned KDC_ERR_PREAUTH_REQUIRED (pre-authentication required) before succeeding, indicating accounts are not configured with 'Do not require Kerberos preauthentication'. No AS-REP roasting tooling strings (AS-REP, GetNPUsers, DontRequirePreAuth) were found in PowerShell script blocks.

The only PowerShell 4104 script blocks matching cookie/token/SAML keywords on scranton.dmevals.local are benign: a Sysinternals readme.ps1 helper (Get-AttributesMask, user pbeesly) and PowerShellGet localized resource strings (PSScriptInfo/Authenticode messages). LSASS process-access events with elevated masks (0x1fffff, 0x1f3fff, 0x101001) originate from legitimate SYSTEM processes (wininit.exe, csrss.exe, svchost.exe) and a SYSTEM-context PowerShell.exe whose call trace is ntdll.dll/KERNELBASE.dll, not a credential-dumping tool. Logon process names are normal (Kerberos 217, Advapi 76, User32 2, NtLmSsp 1). No forged web credential material was observed.
findings.title: No web-credential forging activity; keyword hits are benign PowerShell resource strings

findings.summary: The only Sysmon file-creation event matching a cookie path is C:\Windows\ServiceProfiles\LocalService\AppData\Local\Packages\warp_jit_db4a1097-b484-4973-bbf2-a04208ecd4d4\AC\INetCookies on scranton.dmevals.local, created by C:\windows\System32\svchost.exe (LocalService profile). This is normal Windows service-profile cookie storage, not browser cookie theft or forging. No Set-Cookie/session manipulation was found in PowerShell script blocks.
findings.title: Single cookie-path file event is a benign Windows service-profile INetCookies file

findings.summary: No SAML/Assertion/NotOnOrAfter content appears in any PowerShell 4104 script block (the only keyword matches are PowerShellGet Authenticode resource strings), no saml/token/cert command lines appear in Sysmon process-creation events, and no saml/adfs/token URLs appear in Zeek HTTP requests. The Zeek window (2020-04-30) contains only WebDAV OPTIONS/PROPFIND traffic (user agent Microsoft-WebDAV-MiniRedir) and does not overlap the Windows host windows. No SAML token forging was observed.

findings.title: WMI provider lifecycle events (5857/5858) on newyork.dmevals.local are routine, not MFA request generation
findings.summary: The only T1621 check with hits (C355, windows.other, event.code 5857/5858) returned routine WMI activity on newyork.dmevals.local. Event 5857 records WMI providers starting successfully (result code 0x0) inside wmiprvse.exe (e.g. dsccore, CIMWin32, StorageWMI, SppProvider), and event 5858 records SYSTEM-initiated IWbemServices::DeleteInstance operations against Root\Rsop\Computer RSOP_ExtensionStatus with ResultCode 0x80041002 (object not found) — a normal Group Policy RSOP cleanup pattern. No MFA/2FA/authenticator push, phone-call, or repeated authentication-request artifacts appear in any dataset. There are no 4625 failed-logon events in windows.security, and no MFA-related strings in PowerShell script blocks or Sysmon process command lines.

findings.title: Routine OS certificate-store registry writes by svchost/lsass/taskhostw (benign)
findings.summary: The bulk of the 1133 registry writes matching *Certificate*/*Crypto*/*Keys* are normal Windows certificate-store maintenance: svchost.exe and lsass.exe updating AuthRoot and 'Windows Live ID Token Issuer' certificate Blobs on nashua.dmevals.local, taskhostw.exe writing per-user ACRS PhysicalStores values on scranton.dmevals.local, and smss.exe creating the WOW6432Node SystemCertificates symbolic link. These are system processes, not the attacker's PowerShell, and represent expected certificate-store activity rather than certificate theft or forging.

findings.title: No DHCP spoofing; no DHCP telemetry present in any dataset
findings.summary: No DHCP-related activity is observable. The zeek capture contains no dhcp log type (only conn/files/ssl/x509/dce_rpc/http/dns/kerberos/dpd/smb_files/weird/smb_mapping/notice/pe). windows.other contains no DHCP event codes (1341/1342/1020/1063). Sysmon network connections (event 3) show no DHCP ports 67/68. No DHCP strings appear in PowerShell script blocks. The only broadcast traffic is normal NetBIOS name service (137/138) from System.

incidents.title: LSASS memory access with full-access masks by PowerShell on scranton and wsmprovhost on nashua
incidents.rationale: All these findings anchor on the same LSASS handle-access events: PowerShell.exe (PID 2976, user pbeesly) opening lsass.exe with GrantedAccess 0x1F3FFF/0x1FFFFF on scranton.dmevals.local at 2020-05-02T03:05:16, and wsmprovhost.exe opening lsass.exe with 0x1F3FFF on nashua.dmevals.local at 03:09:29, with matching Security 4656/4663 events showing read-from-process-memory access masks. This is the classic LSASS memory credential-dump pattern, best fitting T1003.001 (LSASS Memory).

incidents.title: lsass.exe writes C:\Windows\debug\PASSWD.LOG on scranton
incidents.rationale: On scranton.dmevals.local, lsass.exe (SYSTEM) created C:\Windows\debug\PASSWD.LOG during the intrusion window, consistent with credential material being written out from LSASS memory, fitting T1003.001 (LSASS Memory).

incidents.title: Sysinternals pspasswd/accesschk credential collection creating 'passwordsDB' on scranton
incidents.rationale: PowerShell (user pbeesly) wrote Sysinternals pspasswd64.exe/pspasswd.exe and ran accesschk.exe, which created the file C:\Program Files\SysinternalsSuite\passwordsDB on scranton.dmevals.local. pspasswd is a password tool and the passwordsDB artifact indicates local account credential material collection, best fitting T1003.002 (Security Account Manager).

incidents.title: Forced authentication via SMB/WebDAV coercion from scranton to attacker-controlled 192.168.0.4
incidents.rationale: Host 10.0.1.4 (scranton.dmevals.local) attempted SMB to 192.168.0.4:445 (rejected) then fell back to WebDAV over HTTP using the Windows WebDAV redirector, issuing OPTIONS/PROPFIND/PUT/LOCK/PROPPATCH/HEAD/UNLOCK with an AUTHORIZATION header. This coerced authentication to an attacker-controlled host is T1187 (Forced Authentication).

incidents.title: Explicit-credential logons (4648) using pbeesly credentials via PsExec
incidents.rationale: Event 4648 explicit-credential logons for pbeesly originating from 10.0.1.6 on scranton and via PSEXESVC.exe on nashua are consistent with reuse of harvested credentials; the credential material itself is used from tooling/scripts, best fitting T1552.001 (Credentials In Files) among in-scope techniques.

incidents.title: Hardcoded credentials in Invoke-Exfil used to mount attacker WebDAV share
incidents.rationale: The Invoke-Exfil PowerShell script block on scranton.dmevals.local contains embedded plaintext credentials ($UserName='cozy', $Password='MyCozyPassw0rd!') used to map \\192.168.0.4\webdav. Credentials embedded in files/scripts fit T1552.001 (Credentials In Files).

incidents.title: Rar.exe password-protected archive of credential-bearing loot on nashua
incidents.rationale: On nashua.dmevals.local, Rar.exe (user pbeesly) created a password-protected archive of collected data, later wiped with sdelete64. This is staging of harvested credential/browser-store data, best fitting T1555.003 (Credentials from Web Browsers).

incidents.title: Anomalous krbtgt service-ticket requests from SCRANTON$ on newyork
incidents.rationale: On newyork.dmevals.local, machine account SCRANTON$ requested Kerberos service tickets for the krbtgt service with TicketOptions 0x60810010, an unusual pattern consistent with forged/abused ticket activity (golden-ticket style), fitting T1558.001.

incidents.title: PowerShell Get-PrivateKeys exports LocalMachine certificates to .pfx files on scranton
incidents.rationale: User pbeesly ran a PowerShell script block defining Get-PrivateKeys that enumerates cert:\LocalMachine and exports every certificate with Export-PfxCertificate to randomly named .pfx files protected by hardcoded password 'saribas', with a resulting .pfx file observed. Stealing authentication certificates fits T1649.

incidents.title: Related malicious activity in window is not network sniffing (PsExec lateral movement, python C2, screen capture)
incidents.rationale: The window contains PsExec64.exe with plaintext credentials to \\NASHUA spawning python.exe via PSEXESVC that beaconed to 192.168.0.4:8443, plus screen capture and steganography decoding and sdelete64 wiping. This is lateral movement/remote services rather than credential access, so out-of-scope:T1021.002 (SMB/Windows Admin Shares).

incidents.title: Intrusion chain on scranton: malicious .scr, hidden PowerShell, Invoke-Exfil, sdelete cleanup
incidents.rationale: A malicious screen-saver .scr launched from explorer.exe spawned cmd.exe and hidden PowerShell that decoded a payload from monkey.png, compiled code with csc.exe, ran Invoke-Discovery/Invoke-Exfil, and deleted the .scr with sdelete64. This is user execution of a malicious file, not credential access, so out-of-scope:T1204 (User Execution).
